    OOM and how to survive it

    After this lesson you can diagnose a CUDA out-of-memory error and apply the right levers — in the right order — to make a run fit without needlessly sacrificing quality.

    Level: intermediate Read time: ~8 min Prerequisites: GPU memory math Verified: 12 Nov 2026

    Sooner or later you'll see CUDA out of memory. It's the most common fine-tuning failure and, armed with the last lesson's memory model, an entirely solvable one. This is the field guide.

    Read the error

    The OOM means the four consumers — weights, gradients, optimizer state, activations — summed to more than your GPU has. Usually it strikes early: on the first backward pass, when activations peak, or at the first optimizer step, when AdamW allocates its state. An OOM deep into a run that was fine for hours almost always means a batch of unusually long sequences arrived — the longest batch sets the peak, so smoke-test with your longest examples first. The fix is to reduce one or more consumers. Below, levers are ordered roughly from "cheapest to quality" to "biggest hammer."

    The levers, in order

    1. Lower the per-device batch size, and restore the effective batch with gradient accumulation. This directly cuts activation memory with no change to training dynamics — almost always the first move.
    2. Enable gradient checkpointing. Instead of storing all activations for the backward pass, it re-computes them on the fly — trading roughly one extra forward pass (about 33% more compute) for a large drop in activation memory. Often the single most effective fix on big models; on small ones the slowdown can outweigh it (on a default small-model run BrewSLM measured 30 s with it vs 19 s without, at the same loss, so its auto setting leaves checkpointing off at 2B parameters and below unless the longest row is over 1,024 tokens).
    3. Reduce max_seq_length if your data allows (recall activations scale with sequence length). Don't clip completions to do it.
    4. Load the frozen base in bf16 if you somehow aren't — that halves weight memory versus fp32 — and train with bf16 mixed precision, which saves activation memory (it keeps fp32 master weights for trained parameters, so it doesn't halve those).
    5. Switch to LoRA if you were full fine-tuning — this removes the base model's gradients and optimizer state, usually the biggest win of all.
    6. Use QLoRA (4-bit quantized base) if even LoRA's weight memory won't fit — quarters the weight footprint.
    7. Lower the LoRA rank / target fewer modules for a final trim.

    Order of operations

    Start with batch size + gradient accumulation and gradient checkpointing — they cost you almost nothing in quality. Only escalate to QLoRA or smaller rank when the cheaper levers run out. Change one lever at a time so you know what worked.

    Why "auto-retry on OOM" exists

    Because OOM is so common, mature training systems automate the levers. BrewSLM, for example, restarts the training attempt after an OOM, up to max_oom_retries times (2 by default; recipes set 1–3), changing one thing each time, in this order: halve the per-device batch and double gradient accumulation; once the batch is 1, shrink max_seq_length to 75%; then turn off packing; then turn off flash attention; then halve the LoRA rank. Knowing the manual levers means you understand exactly what such auto-retry is doing — and can configure it sensibly. Note that the sequence-length step can clip long rows, which is the very thing the caution below warns about: when a run needed a retry, check its log for what changed and how many rows were truncated.

    A caution

    Don't fix OOM by silently truncating completions or dropping hard examples — that trades a crash for a quieter quality bug (recall the truncation warning from the tokenization lesson). The levers above shrink memory without corrupting your data; reach for those first. With memory under control, the next two lessons turn to reading the result: spotting overfitting, and evaluating properly.

    Key terms

    CUDA OOM
    Out-of-memory error when the four memory consumers exceed GPU capacity.
    Gradient checkpointing
    Re-computing activations during backprop instead of storing them — trades compute for big memory savings.
    Batch-size lever
    Lowering per-device batch (then restoring effective batch via accumulation) to cut activation memory without changing dynamics.
    Auto-OOM retry
    Automatically restarting the training attempt with a smaller batch, then a shorter max_seq_length (and further levers) after an OOM, so one oversized batch doesn't kill a run.
